title: Vakataka Kingdom
capsule: The Vakataka dynasty ruled the central Deccan from approximately the mid-third century CE, emerging as the dominant power in the region between the Vindhya range and the Krishna River. Under Pravarasena I (early fourth century) they performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice and styled themselves samrat, signalling imperial ambitions; their alliance with the Gupta dynasty was cemented by the marriage of Rudrasena II to Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, around 385. The dynasty is celebrated for patronising the Ajanta cave paintings during the reign of Harishena (c. 460-478), which represent the apex of classical Indian Buddhist art. The Vakatakas disappear from the record by the mid-sixth century, likely absorbed by the Chalukyas of Badami.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Vakataka territorial extent is reconstructed primarily from copper-plate land-grant inscriptions and stone inscriptions; the core Vidarbha region and Deccan territories are reasonably well delimited, but peripheral zones and the precise chronology of expansion and contraction remain debated among epigraphers.
